title: RBAC v2: add authz conformance test suite (permission declared + check wired) and enforce in CI
author: Leila Farouk
release_notes: Internal: adds CI enforcement to prevent new control-plane/console-backend endpoints from shipping without an RBAC v2 permission declaration and an authorization middleware check.
description: Summary This PR adds an authz conformance test suite that fails CI if a new endpoint is added without (a) a declared RBAC v2 permission and (b) an authz check wired in the handler/middleware chain. Motivation We keep finding “missing check” gaps during the permission inventory and during migration shadow-mode. The intent here is to make the safe path the default: you can’t accidentally ship a new sensitive endpoint with no permission annotation or with an unenforced permission. Scope This is intentionally limited to control-plane HTTP routes and console-backend routes in this first pass. Data-plane inference/auth is out of scope for RBAC v2 phase 1. What’s included - A table-driven conformance test that enumerates registered routes from our route registry (no server startup required) - Assertions per route: (1) permission metadata is present (rbac.Action / permission string), (2) handler chain includes authz middleware (authz.RequirePermission or equivalent), (3) route is classified as exempt only via an explicit allowlist entry with rationale - A small allowlist for endpoints that are intentionally unauthenticated or use different auth primitives (healthz/readyz, metrics, internal probe, oauth callbacks) - A CI job step that runs these conformance tests and surfaces actionable failure output - Developer docs in-repo: how to annotate a route, how to add a valid exemption, and common gotchas Implementation notes - Route enumeration uses the existing router registration map (controlplane/routes/registry) to avoid brittle OpenAPI parsing. We collect: method, path template, owning service/module, permission string (if present), and applied middleware tags. - Middleware detection is done via explicit wrapper helpers that tag the chain (this avoids reflection on closures). For existing authz helpers that didn’t tag, this PR adds tags at the helper boundary only (no behavior change). - Exemptions are versioned in code (internal/authz/conformance/exemptions.yaml) and require a reason + reviewer group in the file header comment. Example failure output (what devs will see) - FAIL authz conformance: POST /v1/orgs/{org_id}/api-keys missing permission declaration; expected route.WithPermission("org.api_keys.write") - FAIL authz conformance: PATCH /v1/orgs/{org_id}/billing/plan has permission org.billing.write but no authz middleware in chain; expected authz.RequirePermission before handler Related - ENG-5381 (RBAC v2 epic) - ENG-5384 (shared authz library) - ENG-5385 (control-plane integration) Follow-ups - Extend to a broader set of internal admin endpoints once we finalize how break-glass routes are represented in the router registry - Consider a lightweight “policy bundle contains permission string” check once policy bundle version pinning is stable across Hosted/Dedicated/Private Checklist - [x] Unit tests for conformance scanner - [x] CI wiring (required check) - [x] Docs for exemptions + route annotation - [x] Verified local developer workflow: conformance test fails with clear output and points to fix
commits: authz/conformance: add route scanner + baseline assertions
routes: tag authz middleware wrappers for conformance detection
ci: run authz conformance tests in required checks
docs: add RBAC v2 route annotation + exemption guidance
conversation: Jordan Lee (review): How are we detecting that the authz middleware is actually in the chain vs just having a permission string? I don’t want this to be easy to bypass accidentally. Leila Farouk (author): Agree. This PR adds a small tag interface at the middleware helper boundary (authz.RequirePermission / authz.RequireAny) and the conformance scanner checks tags on the built route, not the handler body. If someone bypasses helpers and wires a bespoke authz check, they’ll need to add a tag wrapper or add an exemption with rationale (explicitly reviewed). Kaitlyn Nguyen (review): Please ensure we don’t block known-public endpoints (healthz/readyz/metrics) and that exemptions are hard to grow silently. Can we require a reason string + ownership? Leila Farouk (author): Added exemptions.yaml validation: each entry needs reason + owner_group, and the test fails on wildcard patterns other than the approved ones (/healthz, /readyz, /metrics). Also added a doc section on when exemptions are acceptable. Ethan Park (review): Concern about runtime overhead. Are we adding anything to the hot path? Leila Farouk (author): No runtime overhead beyond adding tags inside existing middleware helpers (constant-time metadata). No additional middleware or checks are added. Amara Diallo (review): Console-backend route registry differs from control plane (TS). Is the TS check equivalent? Leila Farouk (author): Equivalent but implemented in TS using the route definition objects; it checks for permission field + presence of requirePermission middleware in the route’s middleware array. Allison Grant (review): Logging/trace: any changes? Leila Farouk (author): None. This PR only adds tags for conformance; structured logging fields remain as in PR #18451. Kaitlyn Nguyen (approval): Looks good with the exemptions validation tightened. Approving. Jordan Lee (approval): Approved. Please track follow-up for break-glass route representation. Ethan Park (approval): Approved. Merge after CI green.
